scenes.heading: letters become postcards
scenes.narration: You send mail every day, so why does the internet survive broken wires. Letters become postcards here, chopped up, sorted alone, then rebuilt for you at the end.

scenes.heading: what the sources say
scenes.narration: What the sources say guides this story. The encyclopedia describes chopping data, joining networks, and the standards body describes later stewardship. Those phrases matter because each fixes one failure.

highlights.quote: splitting it into very short, standardized chunks
multiple separate networks could be joined
transition of the coordination and management

scenes.heading: chop the letter
scenes.narration: Chop the letter first. Packet switching, meaning chopping data into addressed chunks, frees you from one fixed telephone line. If one road closes, your postcards take another road.

board_nodes.evidence: divided into what he called "message blocks"
splitting it into very short, standardized chunks
all users of the network will provide

scenes.heading: join the networks
scenes.narration: Join the networks next. A gateway, meaning a sorting office between networks, reads each postcard address and forwards it onward. Shared rules let old networks stay unchanged yet still deliver to you.

board_nodes.evidence: clouds representing three different packet-switched networks
boxes representing the computers hanging off
Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) and Internet Protocol

scenes.heading: dates show growth
scenes.narration: Dates show growth from experiment to everyday utility. One military network becomes many research networks, then a public backbone, then community stewardship. The turn is from control toward shared care.

items.evidence: ARPA awarded contracts in 1969 for the development
published their research on internetworking in 1974
provided interconnectivity in 1986 with the NSFNET project
Today, 1 October 2016, the contract between the Internet

scenes.heading: share of traffic
scenes.narration: Then the share took off. In 1993 the internet carried one percent of two way traffic. By 2000 it was about half, and by 2007 it carried nearly all of it.

items.evidence: only communicated 1% of the information flowing through two-way telecommunications networks in the year 1993
more than 97% of the telecommunicated information by 2007

scenes.heading: names find pages
scenes.narration: Names find pages for you. The address book, meaning the Domain Name System for finding computers, maps names to numbers. Linked pages then give you mail, calls, shopping, and news without new wires.

board_nodes.evidence: emergence of architecture such as the Domain
linking hypertext documents into an information system
coordination and management of the Internet’s unique identifiers

scenes.heading: postcards still deliver
scenes.narration: Postcards still deliver your internet. Chopped data survives breaks, gateways join networks, and shared names keep it open. Remember that trick, and the growth makes sense.
